guideTitle: Best Streaming Mixers for Xbox Streaming (2026)
metaTitle: Best Streaming Mixers for Xbox Streaming
metaDescription: Six streaming mixers compared for an Xbox stream through a capture card and PC, covering XLR preamps, faders, sound pads and routing limits.
expertTake: The MAONO G3 is the best mixer for an Xbox stream that runs through a PC because its four faders let you balance game capture, chat and microphone separately. The FIFINE Ampligame SC3 is the value pick for a streamer who needs one clean XLR microphone. A console player who streams straight from the Xbox app needs no mixer and should buy a good headset.
introParagraphs: An Xbox stream usually travels through a capture card into a computer, and the mixer sits on the computer side of that chain. Its job is to bring your microphone, the captured game sound and any chat or music together into one clean blend.

That has one important consequence: these are PC audio mixers, not console accessories. Console audio rarely connects to a generic USB mixer directly, so the practical question is how well each box handles the sources that reach your computer.

products.name: MAONO G3 gaming mixer with 4 faders and 3 submixes
products.description:
The G3 suits an Xbox stream because it treats every source on the computer as something that can be put under a fader. The console's audio arrives through the capture card as an ordinary PC source, and the G3 can map it to one of four faders next to the microphone, chat and music. Three submixes then let you give the stream one blend and your headphones another.

The flexibility asks for setup time. Mapping a capture card source takes some care in the companion software, and the box is built around Windows, so a streamer who wants plug and play will find it more than needed. Next to the FIFINE Ampligame SC3 it adds three faders and routing depth, at a higher price tier.

In use, a typical plan is fader one for the captured game, fader two for party chat, fader three for music and fader four for the microphone monitor. Label them with tape, test with a recording before going live and keep the routing profile backed up so a reinstall does not erase an evening of work.
products.bestFor: Console streamers who send game audio through a capture card and want faders for each source.
pros: Four faders map to any PC audio source
Three submixes separate stream and headphone blends
XLR interface for a real microphone
Fast hands on control during a match
cons: Routing takes an evening to learn

products.name: FIFINE Ampligame SC3 gaming mixer with Indi-Fader
products.description:
The SC3 does one job for an Xbox streamer: it puts a proper XLR microphone onto the computer with a slider and a mute button within reach. Plug and play USB means the PC sees it immediately, and the front mounted mute and monitor buttons are easy to hit while holding a controller.

It does not mix the console. Game audio reaches the computer through the capture card and is controlled in software, so the SC3 is only the voice side of the chain. Compared with the MAONO G1 Neo it skips Bluetooth and sound pads, which keeps it cheap and simple.

For a console player the front mute button is the standout. A cough or a family interruption can be silenced with one hand without leaving the game, and the box asks no further attention. It also behaves predictably between sessions, because there are no profiles to restore and no software that has to be running before the stream starts. Use a balanced XLR cable and a boom arm so the microphone stays away from the controller and desk thumps.
products.bestFor: Console streamers who want a clean XLR voice path with a mute button.
pros: One handed mute button on the front
XLR input for a quality microphone
USB plug and play, no driver chase
cons: Voice only, no game audio control

products.name: MAONO G1 Neo gaming mixer with XLR and 48V phantom
products.description:
The G1 Neo pairs a phantom powered XLR input with four custom sound pads and Bluetooth, which makes it a fit for an Xbox streamer who triggers reactions live. Bluetooth can take audio from a phone, which helps with a second device on the desk.

The pads add personality but also buttons to learn. The preamp supports condenser microphones through 48V, which the SC3 does not advertise, and the RGB lighting suits a themed setup. It sits between the SC3 and G3 in features, with a similar control model to the SC3 but more extras.

Load your sound clips once, keep them short and normalize their volume, since a pad that is louder than your voice startles viewers. Check that the captured game audio and the mixer's USB audio do not both feed the stream mix at once.
products.bestFor: Streamers who use a condenser microphone and trigger sound effects.
pros: Four custom pads for sound cues

products.name: FIFINE SC8 gaming mixer with 7.1 surround and RGB
products.description:
The SC8 offers a headphone preamp, 7.1 surround processing, RGB lighting and a mute button. For a streamer who monitors captured game audio on a demanding headset, the preamp helps drive it.

Surround processing is a monitoring feature for the person wearing the headset, not something that changes what viewers hear. Beside the SC3 it adds surround and lighting, but control depth is similar.

Place it where the mute button is reachable and keep the surround setting matched to your headset. If you prefer plain stereo for positional accuracy in competitive shooters, leave the surround processing off. The headphone preamp is the more durable benefit, since a demanding headset sounds weak and thin from a typical onboard output and fuller from a proper amplifier stage. Check that the volume knob has room to spare at your normal listening level.
products.bestFor: Streamers who monitor with a demanding headset and like RGB.
pros: RGB lighting for a themed desk
cons: Surround matters to you, not your audience
Control depth like an entry mixer

products.name: PUPGSIS gaming audio mixer with voice changer

specList.label: Compatibility
specList.value: PC, phone, tablet, PS4 and PS5

products.description:
This PUPGSIS mixer is an all in one audio hub with a voice changer and soundboard. Its listing is clear about a limit: it supports XLR and quarter inch dynamic microphones but not USB microphones or 48V phantom power microphones.

That restriction matters. A condenser microphone will not work, which rules it out for many streamers, while a dynamic microphone is exactly what noisy gaming rooms need. The listing also names PC, phone, tablet and PS4 or PS5 compatibility, but does not mention Xbox, so confirm routing before relying on a console connection.

Choose it if you already own a dynamic microphone and want a voice changer and soundboard at a low price tier. Keep the voice effect for segments, and check the manual for how console audio is meant to be connected. A dynamic microphone with a proper XLR cable gives the best result here, and a pop filter helps a close talking habit. If you later switch to a condenser microphone, plan to replace the mixer as well, since this unit cannot supply the voltage.
products.bestFor: Dynamic microphone owners who want a soundboard and voice changer cheaply.
pros: Supports XLR and TRS dynamic microphones
Compatible with PC, phone and tablet
cons: No 48V phantom or USB mic support

products.name: MAILANGSHI gaming audio mixer with XLR and noise reduction
products.description:
MAILANGSHI's gaming mixer offers an XLR input with 48V phantom power, noise reduction and an easy hands on layout. It is the cheapest board in this group that lists both phantom power and noise reduction.

Details on gain and build are thin, so treat it as a budget option. Against the SC3 it adds phantom power and noise reduction, while the SC3 has a clearer reputation and front controls.

Test the noise reduction with your own voice and room, since aggressive settings can make speech sound processed. Keep a spare cable and avoid placing the box near the console's power brick. Because the noise reduction is aggressive on many budget boards, record the same sentence with it on and off and keep the setting only if the voice still sounds natural. Expect to retune the gain whenever you change microphones.
products.bestFor: Budget streamers who want phantom power and noise reduction.
cons: Little published gain and build detail

buyingCriteria.explanation: A generic USB mixer does not plug into an Xbox as an audio device. The usual path is the console's HDMI output into a capture card, then into the PC, where the mixer works alongside it. Plan the audio route before buying, because a mixer that only handles your microphone is fine for that route, while one with faders helps balance the captured game.

The MAONO G3 has four faders mapped to any PC source, while the SC3 gives one slider for the microphone. If you balance game capture, party chat and music live, faders save time. If you set levels once, a single slider is enough.

The MAONO G1 Neo and MAILANGSHI list 48V phantom power for condensers, while the PUPGSIS only supports dynamic microphones. A noisy room favors a dynamic microphone, and a quiet one can use a condenser. Check the listing against the microphone you own.

You want your headphones to carry party chat and game sound while the stream carries a different blend. The G3's three submixes handle that. Boxes without submixes mix everything together, so chat voices can leak into the broadcast.

A console player holds a controller, so a mute button must be reachable with one hand and without a glance away from the screen. Place the box to the side of the controller hand and mark the mute button with a small piece of tape so you can find it by touch during a tense moment. The SC3 and SC8 have front mute controls. Back mounted switches are awkward in a match and encourage mistakes.

Pads on the G1 Neo and a soundboard on the PUPGSIS trigger effects live. They help a comedy or reaction channel and add little to a serious stream. Weigh the learning curve against how much you will use them.

howWeEvaluated.title: PC side routing
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each mixer fits a capture card and PC chain, noting that none connects directly to an Xbox. The G3's fader mapping handled that route best. A mixer that expects a console cable and offers no PC routing would be a poor match, so we judged every unit on how it handles sources that arrive through the computer.

howWeEvaluated.title: Microphone support
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared XLR support and phantom power, noting the PUPGSIS limit to dynamic microphones. Microphone choice is the biggest influence on how a stream sounds, so a mixer that locks you out of a whole class of microphones loses points even when its other features are good.

howWeEvaluated.title: One handed use
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored front mounted mute and monitor buttons, since a console player holds a controller. A control that needs two hands or a glance away from the screen is a liability in a fast game, and we weighed the location of each button as well as its presence.

howWeEvaluated.title: Extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at pads, Bluetooth and voice effects, rating them as extras rather than essentials. They can lift a channel with a strong personality, but they do not fix a weak microphone path, and a long feature list can hide thin fundamentals.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tiers, with the MAILANGSHI and SC3 at the low end and the G3 higher.

faq.q: Can I plug a mixer into an Xbox?
faq.a: Generic USB mixers do not work as Xbox audio devices. Most streamers route the console through a capture card to a PC, where the mixer handles the microphone and any other sources. That path also lets you add overlays and alerts in streaming software. Check the manual of any mixer before assuming it will talk to a console directly, because listings often name other consoles but not Xbox.

faq.q: Which mixer is best for Xbox streaming?
faq.a: The MAONO G3 is best for balancing capture, chat and voice, because four faders can be mapped to any PC source. The SC3 is best for a simple microphone with a front mute button. A streamer who also wants phantom power and pads should look at the G1 Neo, which sits between the two.

faq.q: Do I need a mixer at all?
faq.a: Not if you stream with the Xbox app and a headset, because the console handles voice and game audio on its own. A mixer becomes useful once you move to a PC based stream with a capture card, an XLR microphone and several audio sources to balance. Until then, a good headset with a clear microphone is the cheapest improvement.

Only for condenser microphones, which need 48V sent over the XLR cable. Dynamic microphones do not need it and are often the better choice in a noisy gaming room. The PUPGSIS mixer does not support phantom power, so it only suits dynamic microphones, while the G1 Neo and MAILANGSHI list 48V.

faq.q: Will party chat leak into my stream?
faq.a: It can without separate mixes. Use submixes so your headphones carry party chat while the stream carries only your voice and the game. The MAONO G3 offers three submixes for exactly this. On simpler boxes, keep chat audio out of the PC route entirely by running it into a separate headset.

They suit comedy and reaction channels, where a quick sound cue is part of the show. For a calm, voice focused stream they add little. If you buy a unit with pads, keep clips short and set their volume below your voice so a stray press never startles viewers.
